quadHead: Four ways Turkey catches tourists off guard.

quad.title: The Fake Police ID Check
quad.tl: Two men near the Grand Bazaar flash laminated badges, claim a counterfeit-currency check, separate your passport from your wallet — and hand the passport back short of cash.

quad.title: The Grand Bazaar Upsell
quad.tl: Apple tea and a family-weaving story seat you for 45–90 minutes; the carpet opens at 8,000 lira and drops theatrically to 3,000 when you stand — still double the street price.

quad.title: The Barlar Sokağı Bill Shock
quad.tl: A friendly local walks you to a Bar Street club; after a few rounds a €200–€800 bill arrives and bouncers block the exit until you pay.

quad.title: The Kaleiçi Taxi Meter Trick
quad.tl: Drivers refuse the meter or quote in euros — a ₺350–₺500 airport run becomes a €25–€40 flat rate (₺750–₺1,200) at the arrivals exit.

body: Turkey: Tourist Scams is part of the tabiji.ai Travel Safety Series. Every scam is documented — not recycled — against Turkish police (155) and Jandarma (156) bulletins, TÜRSAB and Consumer Arbitration Committee complaints, Daily Sabah and Hürriyet Daily News reporting, and firsthand traveler accounts.

78 specific scams across Istanbul, Cappadocia, Antalya, Bodrum and nine more destinations. The exact scripts, the red flags that give them away, and the Turkish phrases that shut them down — written in Latin script you can show on your phone.

Scams evolve, so the book is re-researched and updated every year — when a new edition ships, it appears in your Kindle library. Built for the traveler who wants to move through Turkey relaxed, not braced.
